description: Core Java and the modern language features that show up in production services and interviews: equality and hashing, collections, generics, exceptions, streams and collectors, Optional, records, sealed types, and pattern matching. Timeline follows Oracle: var in 10, switch expressions in 14, text blocks in 15, records and instanceof patterns in 16, sealed classes in 17, pattern matching for switch and record patterns final in 21.

cards.front: Why does == sometimes work for two Integers and sometimes not?
cards.back: Integer caches values from -128 to 127. == compares references, so cached boxes can be the same object. Outside that range they are different objects with the same value.
cards.explanation: Always use equals for value comparison of wrapper types. The cache is a JVM optimization, not a language rule you should depend on. Unboxing a null Integer throws NullPointerException.
cards.example: Integer a = 200; Integer b = 200; a == b is false. a.equals(b) is true. Integer x = 10; Integer y = 10; x == y is true only because both came from the cache.

cards.front: What is the equals and hashCode contract, and what breaks if you violate it?
cards.back: If a.equals(b), then a.hashCode() must equal b.hashCode(). Unequal objects may share a hash code. HashMap and HashSet use the hash to find a bucket, then equals to find the object.
cards.explanation: If two equal objects have different hash codes, a HashMap lookup misses the entry. If you override equals and forget hashCode, the object is lost inside sets and maps. Include the same fields in both methods. Do not use mutable fields that change while the object is a map key.
cards.example: A User with equals based on email but a default identity hashCode cannot be retrieved from a HashSet after insertion.

cards.front: Is Java pass-by-reference?
cards.back: No. Java passes arguments by value. For objects, the value is a copy of the reference.
cards.explanation: A method can mutate the object the reference points at, which looks like pass-by-reference. Reassigning the parameter (user = new User()) does not change the caller's variable. This distinction matters when reading code that 'swaps' two objects and silently fails.
cards.example: void rename(User u) { u.name = "Ava"; } changes the caller. void replace(User u) { u = new User(); } does not.

cards.front: Why is String immutable, and what does that buy you in a large codebase?
cards.back: A String's contents never change. Concatenation creates a new String. Immutability makes Strings safe to share, safe as map keys, and eligible for the string pool.
cards.explanation: Security and concurrency rely on this: a class name or a password passed as a String cannot be mutated by another thread. For many concatenations in a loop, use StringBuilder. The pool means identical literals can share one instance, which is why == sometimes appears to work on literals and must still not be used.
cards.example: String s = "hi"; s.concat("!") does not change s. You must assign the result.

cards.front: What is the difference between a checked exception and a runtime exception, and how do companies usually use them?
cards.back: Checked exceptions extend Exception but not RuntimeException and must be caught or declared. Runtime exceptions signal programmer errors or unrecoverable states and are unchecked.
cards.explanation: Checked exceptions force callers to notice recoverable cases such as a missing file. Overusing them makes APIs noisy, so many codebases wrap infrastructure failures in unchecked exceptions at the boundary and keep checked exceptions rare. Never catch Exception and swallow it. Catch the narrowest type you can handle, and add context when you wrap.
cards.example: IOException is checked. IllegalArgumentException and NullPointerException are unchecked.

cards.front: What does try-with-resources guarantee that a hand-written finally block often gets wrong?
cards.back: It closes every AutoCloseable in reverse order of creation, even when the body throws, and it suppresses close-time exceptions onto the original exception.
cards.explanation: A manual finally that closes a stream can throw and hide the real bug. Try-with-resources keeps the primary exception and attaches the close failure as a suppressed exception. Use it for JDBC connections, streams, and HttpClient response bodies. If you forget, connection pools exhaust under load — a classic production incident.
cards.example: try (var in = Files.newBufferedReader(path)) { return in.readLine(); }

cards.front: When do you choose ArrayList over LinkedList?
cards.back: Choose ArrayList almost always. It is an array: get is O(1), add at the end is amortized O(1). LinkedList get is O(n) and each node costs extra memory.
cards.explanation: LinkedList looks attractive for insert-in-the-middle, but you must already hold the node. Finding the index is O(n), so the theoretical win disappears. ArrayList's contiguous memory is also friendlier to CPU caches. Use LinkedList only when you truly add and remove at the ends and profiling says the array is the problem — which is rare.
cards.example: A list of 100_000 orders: list.get(50_000) is instant on ArrayList and walks 50_000 nodes on LinkedList.

cards.front: How does HashMap find a key, and what is the load factor for?
cards.back: It hashes the key, picks a bucket, then walks that bucket comparing equals. The default load factor is 0.75. When size exceeds capacity times 0.75, the map resizes and rehashes.
cards.explanation: A bad hashCode puts every key in one bucket and lookup becomes O(n). Since Java 8, long bucket chains of Comparable keys become trees, which limits the damage but does not fix a constant hashCode. One null key is allowed. Null values are allowed. Do not share a plain HashMap across threads without external locking — that can corrupt the structure.
cards.example: new HashMap<>(expectedSize) avoids repeated resizes when you know the size in advance.

cards.front: What is wrong with returning Optional from a field, or calling optional.get() immediately?
cards.back: Optional is a return type for a value that may be absent. get() throws if it is empty. Prefer orElse, orElseGet, orElseThrow, map, or ifPresent.
cards.explanation: Optional is not Serializable in a useful way and should not be a JPA field or a JSON property. orElse(expensive()) always evaluates the argument. orElseGet(() -> expensive()) evaluates it only when empty. Never use Optional.of(nullable) — that throws if the value is null. Use ofNullable.
cards.example: return userRepo.findByEmail(email).orElseThrow(() -> new NotFoundException(email));

cards.front: Are streams evaluated immediately?
cards.back: No. Intermediate operations (filter, map, sorted) are lazy. Nothing runs until a terminal operation (collect, count, findFirst, reduce).
cards.explanation: You can build a pipeline that is never executed if you forget the terminal call. Side effects inside map are a design smell because retries or parallel() may run them more than once or not at all in the way you expect. Streams are single-use. Parallel streams use the common ForkJoinPool and can starve other tasks or lose ordering. Use them only for CPU-heavy, independent work on large in-memory data — not for JDBC calls.
cards.example: names.stream().filter(n -> n.startsWith("A")).map(String::toUpperCase).toList();

cards.front: What does type erasure mean for generics?
cards.back: At runtime, List<String> and List<Integer> are both just List. The compiler checks the type arguments, then erases them.
cards.explanation: You cannot write new T(), cannot overload methods that differ only by a generic parameter, and cannot do instanceof List<String>. This is why a library method sometimes takes Class<T> explicitly. Heap pollution happens when raw types or unchecked casts put the wrong object in a generic collection. The compiler warning is telling you a ClassCastException may happen far from the bug.
cards.example: List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(); at runtime the JVM does not store 'String' on the list object.

cards.front: When do you use Comparable, and when do you use Comparator?
cards.back: Comparable is the class's natural order (compareTo). Comparator is an external, often one-off order.
cards.explanation: A class should have one natural order, or none. Users sorted by name in one screen and by created date in another need two Comparators, not a changing compareTo. compareTo must be consistent with equals if the objects go into a TreeSet, or the set will drop equal-looking elements. Comparator.comparing(User::email) is the usual Java 8+ form.
cards.example: users.sort(Comparator.comparing(User::createdAt).thenComparing(User::id));

cards.front: Where do local variables live, and where do objects live?
cards.back: Local variables and call frames live on the stack. Objects and arrays live on the heap. The stack holds a reference to the heap object.
cards.explanation: Stack allocation is cheap and dies with the method. The heap is garbage-collected. A common leak is a static List or a listener that keeps heap objects reachable forever, so GC cannot collect them. OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space means the heap is full of reachable objects or you sized -Xmx too small. StackOverflowError means unbounded recursion or huge stack frames, not a heap leak.
cards.example: A static Map<RequestId, byte[]> used as a cache with no eviction will grow until the heap is exhausted.

cards.front: Why is double the wrong type for money?
cards.back: Binary floating point cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly. 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3.
cards.explanation: Use BigDecimal with a String constructor, or store integer minor units (cents). new BigDecimal(0.1) already carries the double's error. new BigDecimal("0.1") does not. Set a scale and a rounding mode at API boundaries. Equality on BigDecimal considers scale: 1.0 and 1.00 are not equal with equals, but compareTo says they are.
cards.example: new BigDecimal("10.00").add(new BigDecimal("0.10"));

cards.front: What is the difference between Instant, LocalDateTime, and ZonedDateTime?
cards.back: Instant is a point on the UTC timeline. LocalDateTime is a date and time with no offset. ZonedDateTime is a local date-time plus a time zone.
cards.explanation: Store instants in the database (UTC). Convert to a zone only for display. LocalDateTime '2026-03-08T02:30' is ambiguous or missing on a daylight-saving transition. Do not use java.util.Date or Calendar in new code. Clock injection makes tests deterministic: Clock.fixed(instant, zone).
cards.example: Instant occurredAt = Instant.now(clock); ZonedDateTime local = occurredAt.atZone(ZoneId.of("America/Toronto"));

cards.front: What does var actually infer, and where is it illegal?
cards.back: var infers the compile-time type of a local variable from the initializer. It is not a keyword you can use for fields, method parameters (except lambdas), or a method return type.
cards.explanation: Local-variable type inference arrived in Java 10 and is what Java 11 codebases mean by var. Java 11 added var for lambda parameters, which matters when you need an annotation on that parameter. var does not change runtime types and is not dynamic typing. Avoid var when the initializer is a diamond or a method whose return type is not obvious on the line — reviewers should not have to jump to a signature to know the type.
cards.example: var users = new ArrayList<User>(); // users is ArrayList<User>, not List<User>. Map.Entry<String, List<User>> e = ... may be clearer than var.

cards.front: Which String methods showed up for everyday Java 11 code?
cards.back: isBlank, lines, strip, stripLeading, stripTrailing, and repeat. isBlank is true for empty or whitespace-only strings. strip removes Unicode whitespace. trim only removes code points <= U+0020.
cards.explanation: lines() splits on \n, \r, or \r\n and does not give you a giant intermediate array the way some split calls do. isBlank is the check you want for a form field. Do not confuse strip with intern or with substring, which no longer shares the old char array (that copy-on-substring change was Java 7).
cards.example: "  hi  ".strip() is "hi". "\n".isBlank() is true. "ha".repeat(3) is "hahaha".

cards.front: What replaced the old HttpURLConnection style in Java 11?
cards.back: java.net.http.HttpClient, HttpRequest, and HttpResponse. The client is immutable and thread-safe. Calls can be sync (send) or async (sendAsync).
cards.explanation: Build one client and reuse it. A client holds a connection pool and threads. Creating one per request defeats that. Timeouts belong on the client or the request. BodyHandlers.ofString() is fine for small payloads. For large ones, stream. This API was incubated before 11 and is standard from 11, so you do not need an external HTTP library for simple service-to-service calls.
cards.example: HttpRequest req = HttpRequest.newBuilder(uri).timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2)).header("Accept", "application/json").GET().build();

cards.front: How do switch expressions differ from the classic switch statement?
cards.back: Arrow labels do not fall through. A switch expression must be exhaustive and produces a value. There is no need for break between arrow cases.
cards.explanation: Switch expressions became permanent in Java 14, so they are normal Java 17 code. Colon labels can still fall through, which is why teams prefer arrows. Use yield to return a value from a block. Missing an enum constant is a compile error for an expression, which beats a production bug from a forgotten break. Pattern matching inside switch is not this feature: that stayed preview in 17 and became standard only in Java 21.
cards.example: int size = switch (level) { case JUNIOR -> 1; case MID -> 2; case SENIOR -> 3; };

cards.front: What problem do text blocks solve?
cards.back: They are multiline string literals delimited by triple quotes. You stop escaping every quote in JSON, SQL, or HTML embedded in tests.
cards.explanation: Final since Java 15. Incidental indentation is stripped to the least-indented line. Trailing spaces can be kept with \s. A text block is still a String. It does not interpolate variables (that was a later preview, string templates, and it was withdrawn). Use text blocks for fixtures. Do not build SQL by concatenating user input into a text block — parameterization is still required.

cards.front: What does a record give you that a hand-written class usually gets wrong?
cards.back: A record is a transparent carrier of immutable data. The compiler writes the canonical constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode, and toString from the components.
cards.explanation: Records are final and cannot extend another class. Components are final. They are the right model for DTOs, map keys, and messages. They are a poor JPA entity: no no-arg constructor for you to control, no setters, and inheritance is limited. Compact constructors are for validation: if (qty < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException(); You can still add methods. Do not mutate hidden cached state and expect equals to stay stable.
cards.example: public record Money(BigDecimal amount, Currency currency) { public Money { if (amount == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException(); } }

cards.front: How does pattern matching for instanceof remove a cast?
cards.back: if (value instanceof Order order) binds order only when the test is true, and the variable is in scope in that branch.
cards.explanation: Permanent since Java 16. The scope is flow-sensitive: inside the if, order is definitely an Order. In the else, it is not in scope. This removes the cast-and-hope ClassCastException pattern. It does not inspect record components by itself. Deconstructing records in patterns is a Java 21 feature. Combining this with sealed types lets a switch or a chain of instanceof checks be exhaustive.
cards.example: if (event instanceof PaymentFailed failed) { retry(failed.orderId()); }

cards.front: What does a sealed class restrict, and why do API designers want that?
cards.back: A sealed type lists the only permitted subtypes with permits. Each permitted type must be final, sealed, or non-sealed.
cards.explanation: Sealed classes are the Java 17 language feature (JEP 409). The superclass can be public while the set of subtypes stays closed. That models a domain sum: a Payment is a Card or a Wallet, and nothing else. Callers can switch on the subtypes and the compiler notices a missing one when you use patterns that support exhaustiveness. An open class hierarchy cannot give you that guarantee. Do not seal a type you expect other teams to extend.
cards.example: public sealed interface Result permits Success, Failure {}

cards.front: Can you use pattern matching in switch on Java 17 in production?
cards.back: Not as a finished feature. JEP 406 made it a preview in 17. It requires --enable-preview and may still change. It became permanent in Java 21 (JEP 441).
cards.explanation: Preview features are not a promise. A library compiled with a preview flag can break on the next JDK. Companies on the Java 17 LTS should use sealed types, records, text blocks, switch expressions, and instanceof patterns, and wait until 21 for switch patterns and record patterns. If an interview asks 'what is new in 17', say sealed classes, and be precise about what was finalized earlier but ships in the 17 LTS.
cards.example: javac --enable-preview --release 17 is a signal you are off the stable language.

cards.front: What changed about NullPointerException messages in modern JDKs?
cards.back: Since Java 14, the JVM can say which part of a chain was null: 'Cannot invoke String.length() because name is null' instead of a line number alone.
cards.explanation: JEP 358 helpful NPE messages are on by default in Java 15+ and therefore on Java 17. They do not prevent the bug. They make the stack trace point at order.getUser().name when user was null, not at a mysterious bytecode index. You still want validation at boundaries and Optional or explicit checks where absence is normal.
cards.example: user.address().city().name() — the message names the first null segment.

cards.front: What should a unit test assert, and what should it leave to an integration test?
cards.back: A unit test checks one behavior of one type, with collaborators faked: given this input, the output or the interaction is that. An integration test checks real wiring: database, HTTP, transactions.
cards.explanation: Asserting every internal call makes the test a change-detector that fails on refactors. Assert observable behavior. Do not hit the network in a unit test. For a pure pricing function, table-driven tests are enough. For a repository, use a real database in an integration test rather than mocking JDBC. Flaky tests that depend on time or order are bugs. Inject a Clock and avoid Thread.sleep.
cards.example: assertThat(pricing.total(cart)).isEqualByComparingTo("19.99");

cards.front: What does an interface give you that an abstract class does not, in modern Java?
cards.back: A type can implement several interfaces and only extend one class. Interfaces can have default and static methods, but they cannot hold instance state.
cards.explanation: Default methods let a library add a method without breaking implementors, if the default is sensible. They are not a reason to build a deep inheritance tree. Prefer composition: a small interface plus a class that holds collaborators. Abstract classes still help when subclasses share protected state or a template method that must not be copied. If you are choosing for a new API, start with an interface.
cards.example: interface Payments { Receipt charge(Money amount); } The HTTP client and the repository sit in the implementing class, not in the interface.

cards.front: Why can a seemingly correct override of equals break in a subclass?
cards.back: Symmetry: if child.equals(parent) is true, parent.equals(child) must be true. A subclass that adds a field and uses instanceof usually breaks that.
cards.explanation: Prefer composition over inheritance for value types, or make the class final, or use a record. If you must extend, some codebases use a canEqual hook. The interview-quality answer is: getters-and-instanceof equals is unsafe across a hierarchy, and this is one reason records (which are final) are a better value type.
cards.example: ColorPoint extending Point and comparing the extra color field fails symmetry with a plain Point at the same coordinates.

cards.front: What belongs in a Java 17 service's public API versus its internals?
cards.back: Public API: small interfaces, records for inputs and outputs, explicit exceptions, no leaked mutable collections. Internals: HashMap, streams, executors.
cards.explanation: Return List.copyOf or an unmodifiable list so callers cannot mutate your cache. Accept interfaces (List) but do not promise a mutable ArrayList. Keep framework annotations off domain records when you can map at the edge. This is the mid-level bar: the code works, and the next team can change the inside without breaking callers.
cards.example: public List<Order> findOpen() { return List.copyOf(open); }

cards.front: What does pattern matching for switch look like in Java 21, and why does it pair with sealed types?
cards.back: switch can match on types and deconstruct them: case Circle c -> ..., case Square s when s.side() > 10 -> .... With a sealed interface, the compiler knows every subtype, so the switch can be exhaustive without a default branch.
cards.explanation: Final in Java 21 (preview in 17-20). If someone adds a new permitted subtype, every exhaustive switch fails to compile until it handles the new case, which is exactly the safety you want for domain states. 'case null' is also allowed.
cards.example: sealed interface Payment permits Card, Iban {}  double fee(Payment p) { return switch (p) { case Card c -> c.amount() * 0.029; case Iban i -> 0.35; }; }

cards.front: What are record patterns (Java 21)?
cards.back: Patterns that deconstruct a record into its components directly in instanceof or switch, including nested records.
cards.explanation: They remove accessor noise for data-oriented code. You can use var in nested patterns and ignore components you don't need.
cards.example: if (obj instanceof Point(int x, int y)) { ... }  case Order(var id, Customer(var name, var tier)) when tier == GOLD -> ...

cards.front: What are sequenced collections (Java 21)?
cards.back: New interfaces SequencedCollection, SequencedSet, and SequencedMap give a uniform API for collections with a defined order: getFirst(), getLast(), addFirst(), addLast(), removeFirst(), removeLast(), and reversed().
cards.explanation: Before 21, getting the last element differed for List (list.get(list.size() - 1)), Deque (getLast()), and LinkedHashSet (iterate to the end). List, Deque, LinkedHashSet, LinkedHashMap, and sorted collections now implement them.
cards.example: var newest = events.getLast(); for (var e : events.reversed()) { ... }

cards.front: What's the difference between Stream.toList() and collect(Collectors.toList())?
cards.back: stream.toList() (Java 16) returns an unmodifiable list. collect(Collectors.toList()) returns a list with no guarantees about mutability (in practice an ArrayList).
cards.explanation: Switching from one to the other can break code that later calls add() on the result: it throws UnsupportedOperationException. Use Collectors.toCollection(ArrayList::new) when you need a mutable list.
cards.example: List<String> names = users.stream().map(User::name).toList(); names.add("x"); // throws

cards.front: Which Collectors should you know for grouping and maps?
cards.back: groupingBy(classifier) for Map<K, List<V>>, with a downstream collector like counting(), summingInt(), or mapping(). partitioningBy(predicate) for true/false groups. toMap(key, value, merge) — without a merge function it throws on duplicate keys.
cards.explanation: toMap with duplicate keys throws IllegalStateException, a common production surprise when data isn't as unique as assumed. groupingBy returns a HashMap; pass a map supplier like TreeMap::new for sorted keys.
cards.example: Map<Status, Long> counts = orders.stream().collect(groupingBy(Order::status, counting()));

cards.front: What do List.of, Set.of, Map.of, and List.copyOf give you?
cards.back: Unmodifiable collections (Java 9+, copyOf Java 10+). They reject nulls (NullPointerException), and Set.of / Map.of reject duplicates at creation (IllegalArgumentException).
cards.explanation: Collections.unmodifiableList is only a read-only view: changes to the original list show through. List.copyOf takes a real snapshot, which is what you want for defensive copies in constructors and records.
cards.example: record Team(String name, List<String> members) { Team { members = List.copyOf(members); } }

cards.front: Why are default methods in interfaces useful, and what's the conflict rule?
cards.back: They let you add methods to an interface without breaking existing implementations (that's how List.sort and Map.forEach were added). If a class inherits the same default method from two interfaces, it must override it and can call a specific one with InterfaceName.super.method().
cards.explanation: Class methods always win over interface defaults. Interfaces can also have static and private methods (Java 9+) to share helper code.
cards.example: interface Auditable { default String auditLabel() { return getClass().getSimpleName(); } }

cards.front: How should you chain Optional instead of calling isPresent() and get()?
cards.back: Use map, flatMap, filter, orElse, orElseGet, orElseThrow, and ifPresentOrElse. Use orElseGet(() -> ...) instead of orElse(expensive()) because orElse always evaluates its argument.
cards.explanation: Optional is meant for return types. Don't use it for fields, method parameters, or collections (return an empty list instead).
cards.example: String city = userRepo.findById(id).map(User::address).map(Address::city).orElse("unknown");

cards.text: Two equal objects must return the same {{c1::hashCode}}.
cards.extra: The reverse is not required. Different objects may share a hash code. Hash-based collections depend on this direction of the contract.

cards.text: Use Optional.{{c1::ofNullable}} when the value might be null.
A Java record's components are implicitly {{c1::final}}.
cards.extra: Records are themselves final. They model immutable data, not entities with a changing lifecycle.

cards.text: A sealed type must declare its permitted subtypes with {{c1::permits}}.
cards.extra: Each permitted subtype is final, sealed, or non-sealed. This is the stable Java 17 feature, JEP 409.

cards.text: Arrow switch cases do not {{c1::fall through}}.
cards.extra: Classic colon cases still fall through unless you break. Switch expressions have been standard since Java 14.

cards.text: {{c1::strip}} removes Unicode whitespace. trim does not.
cards.extra: Java 11. isBlank treats whitespace-only strings as blank. lines() splits a multiline string into a stream.
